slavic_zorya.name: guard the sun-god's white horses
slavic_zorya.notes: The Zoryas dwell in the Palace of the Sun and tend the white horses of Dazhbog the sun, releasing them at dawn and stabling them at dusk.

sources.reference: Slavic folklore of the Zorya (Zaria) sisters; Ralston, Songs of the Russian People

songhai_harakoy_dikko.name: mother and chief of the river-spirits (Tooru)
songhai_harakoy_dikko.notes: Harakoy Dikko is the mistress of the Niger and mother (or wife/consort) of the principal Tooru nobles of the Songhay-Zarma spirit pantheon, a multiethnic line because she bore children to mortals of many peoples.

sources.reference: Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)
Paul Stoller, Fusion of the Worlds (1989)

songhai_harakoy_dikko.name: command the Zin (water-genies) of the river
songhai_harakoy_dikko.notes: She sails the Niger in a great copper canoe propelled by Zin who take various forms at her bidding.

sources.reference: Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)

songhai_cirey.name: wield the lightning and (in some accounts) wisdom
songhai_cirey.notes: Cirey/Kyirey, a Tooru of the storm whose name means 'red', is the spirit of the lightning-flash, named among the seven principal Tooru alongside Dongo the thunder.

sources.reference: Paul Stoller, Fusion of the Worlds (1989); Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)

songhai_manda_hausakoy.name: forge iron at the spirit-world anvil
songhai_manda_hausakoy.notes: Manda Hausakoy is the smith of the Tooru, master of the forge; in possession ceremonies the Hausakoy spirit mounts a medium and works as the divine blacksmith, patron of the smith-caste.

sources.reference: Paul Stoller, Fusion of the Worlds (1989); Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)

songhai_faran_maka.name: wield the strength of a giant
songhai_faran_maka.notes: Faran Maka Bote grew into a giant of vast bodily power and magic, the only being able to master the Niger's spirits.

sources.reference: Songhay oral epic of Faran Maka; Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)

songhai_faran_maka.name: win mastery of the Niger by defeating Zinkibaru
songhai_faran_maka.notes: He battled the water-spirit Zinkibaru for control of the river-creatures and won, seizing the spirit's magic guitar and with it command of the Niger's fish and beasts.

sources.reference: Songhay oral epic of Faran Maka and Zinkibaru

songhai_zinkibaru.name: charm the river-creatures with the magic guitar
songhai_zinkibaru.notes: The blind water-spirit Zinkibaru (Zin Kibaru) owned a magic guitar/lute whose music commanded all the fish and beasts of the Niger, until Faran Maka defeated him and took it.

sources.reference: Songhay oral epic; Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)

sotho_tswana_badimo.name: bless, protect and punish the living kin
sotho_tswana_badimo.notes: The badimo (ancestral dead) regulate moral order, send blessing, fertility and protection when honoured and misfortune or illness when neglected, as intermediaries to Modimo.

sources.reference: I. Schapera, The Tswana; ethnography of Sotho-Tswana ancestor religion

sotho_tswana_modimo.name: create and order the world from above
sotho_tswana_modimo.notes: Modimo, 'the One Above', is the remote, formless, genderless creator and sustainer of all, approached not directly but through the badimo.

sources.reference: E. W. Smith (ed.), African Ideas of God; Tswana/Sotho high-god ethnography

sotho_tswana_senkatana.name: slay the all-swallowing monster Kgodumodumo
sotho_tswana_senkatana.notes: Born to the one pregnant woman the monster had not swallowed, Senkatana grew rapidly to manhood, killed Kgodumodumo and cut open its belly, releasing all the people and animals it had devoured.

sources.reference: Basotho oral legend of Senkatana/Ditaolane; S. M. Mofokeng, Senkatana (1952)

songhai_dongo.name: rule the sky as master of thunder and rain
songhai_dongo.notes: Dongo, the most feared of the Tooru, is master of the sky, responsible for thunder, lightning and the rain that the yenaandi (rain-dance) rites summon for the Songhay-Zarma.

sources.reference: Paul Stoller, Fusion of the Worlds (1989); Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)

suludnon_kaptan.name: rule as supreme sky-god over the lesser deities
suludnon_kaptan.notes: Kaptan (Captan) is the highest sky-deity of the Suludnon and wider Visayan pantheon; his decree that his daughter Alunsina must wed on reaching maidenhood sets the Hinilawod in motion.

sources.reference: F. Landa Jocano, Sulod Society (1968); Outline of Philippine Mythology

suludnon_alunsina.name: give her jewels to become the heavenly bodies
suludnon_alunsina.notes: In the Panay creation account Alunsina's necklace becomes the stars, her comb the moon and her crown the sun, set in the sky by Tungkung Langit in his longing for her.

sources.reference: F. Landa Jocano, collected Panay creation myth of Tungkung Langit and Alunsina

tagalog_amanikable.name: raise tempests and angry seas
tagalog_amanikable.notes: Spurned by the mortal maiden Maganda, the ill-tempered sea-god sends storms, high waves and shipwreck against humankind; an older tradition makes him the god of hunters before he became ruler of the sea.

sources.reference: Tagalog mythology (first-generation deities of the Bathala pantheon); F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology

tagalog_anagolay.name: restore what is lost
tagalog_anagolay.notes: As goddess of lost things Anagolay was invoked to recover misplaced or missing objects; daughter of Ikapati (Lakapati) and Mapulon and wife of Dumakulem.

sources.reference: Tagalog mythology; F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology

tagalog_anitun_tabu.name: govern the wind and the rain
tagalog_anitun_tabu.notes: The fickle-minded goddess of wind and rain rules the weather; in Zambales tradition (as Aniton Tauo) she was once supreme but, grown vain, was demoted by Malayari.

sources.reference: Tagalog and Zambal mythology (Anitun Tabu / Aniton Tauo)

tagalog_dumakulem.name: guard the mountains as their hunter-warden
tagalog_dumakulem.notes: Dumakulem is the strong, agile guardian of the mountains, a robust hunter; son of Idianale and Dimangan and husband of Anagolay.

sources.reference: Tagalog mythology; F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology

tagalog_dimangan.name: grant the good harvest
tagalog_dimangan.notes: Dimangan (Dumangan) is the god of the good harvest, husband of Idianale, who gives abundance to the fields.

sources.reference: Tagalog mythology; F. Landa Jocano, Outline of Philippine Mythology

tagalog_diyan_masalanta.name: grant love, conception and safe childbirth
tagalog_diyan_masalanta.notes: Goddess of love, conception and childbirth and protectress of lovers; the youngest of the deities, daughter of Anagolay and Dumakulem.

sources.reference: J. de Plasencia, Customs of the Tagalogs (1589)

tagalog_apolaki.name: drive the sun and lead warriors in battle
tagalog_apolaki.notes: Son of Bathala, Apolaki rules the day as sun-god and is patron of warriors; in his duel with his sister Mayari over dominion of the earth he blinds her in one eye, so the moon shines fainter than the sun.

songhai_harakoy_dikko.name: yenaandi rain-festival and riverside offerings to the river-mother
songhai_harakoy_dikko.cadence: seasonal (onset of the rains) and at need
songhai_harakoy_dikko.notes: Harakoy Dikko, mistress of the Niger and mother of the Tooru, receives offerings at the riverside and is called down in the holey possession ceremonies; she figures in the yenaandi (rain-making) rites of the Songhay-Zarma.

sources.reference: Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960); Paul Stoller, Fusion of the Worlds (1989)

songhai_manda_hausakoy.name: holey possession-rite of the smith-spirit
songhai_manda_hausakoy.notes: In the Songhay holey ceremonies the smith-spirit Manda Hausakoy mounts a medium and is honoured as patron of the blacksmith-caste and master of the forge.

sources.reference: Paul Stoller, Fusion of the Worlds (1989)

songhai_cirey.name: holey possession-rite of the lightning Tooru
songhai_cirey.cadence: at storm-crisis and seasonal possession rites
songhai_cirey.notes: Cirey/Kyirey, the lightning Tooru, is called down with Dongo in the holey possession dances to the godji fiddle and drums.

sources.reference: Paul Stoller, Fusion of the Worlds (1989)

sotho_tswana_badimo.name: ancestral offerings (go phasa) at the kgotla, grave and cattle-kraal
sotho_tswana_badimo.cadence: at illness, misfortune, lifecycle rites and seasonal need
sotho_tswana_badimo.notes: The badimo are propitiated with libations of beer and the slaughter of an ox or goat at the homestead, kraal or grave; the diviner (ngaka) reads their will, and neglect is held to bring sickness.

sources.reference: I. Schapera, The Tswana; ethnography of Sotho-Tswana ancestor rites

sotho_tswana_modimo.name: approached only through the ancestors; rain-prayer in extremity
sotho_tswana_modimo.notes: Modimo is too remote for an image-cult and is normally approached through the badimo; direct appeal (e.g. communal rain-prayer through the chief) is made only in great need.

sources.reference: E. W. Smith (ed.), African Ideas of God; Sotho-Tswana high-god ethnography

tagalog_bathala.name: offerings to Bathala through anito intermediaries; no temples
tagalog_bathala.notes: Pre-Hispanic Tagalogs built no temples to Bathala; he was venerated through the anito (ancestral/nature spirits) with food-offerings, and his will was read from the flight of the omen-bird tigmamanukan.

sources.reference: J. de Plasencia, Customs of the Tagalogs (1589); A. de Morga, Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas (1609)

tagalog_diyan_masalanta.name: patroness of lovers, conception and safe childbirth
tagalog_diyan_masalanta.notes: Diyan Masalanta was invoked by lovers and by women in childbirth as goddess of love and conception; Plasencia names her as the protectress of lovers whose worship the friars most sought to suppress.

sources.reference: J. de Plasencia, Customs of the Tagalogs (1589)

tagalog_hanan.name: honoured at the first prayer of each day and at life-transitions
tagalog_hanan.cadence: daily at dawn; at birth, adulthood, death, planting and harvest
tagalog_hanan.notes: Hanan, goddess of morning and new beginnings, was invoked at the first prayer of each day alongside Bathala and Apolaki, and especially at life-transitions and the turn of the year.

sources.reference: Tagalog oral tradition of the Bathala daughters

sundanese_nyi_pohaci.name: rice-planting and harvest rites of the rice-mother
sundanese_nyi_pohaci.notes: As the soul of the rice, Nyi Pohaci Sanghyang Asri is honoured in Sundanese (and Javanese-Balinese) rice-planting and harvest ceremonies that guard the crop she became; offerings accompany the seedling and the first sheaf.

sources.reference: Wawacan Sulanjana; Sundanese agrarian ritual (cf. Dewi Sri cult)

attributes.name: white-bearded smith with hammer
attributes.notes: Folk and reconstructed imagery shows Svarog as an aged smith with long white beard wielding hammer and tongs at the heavenly forge.

sources.reference: Slavic folk-tradition of the heavenly smith; Hypatian/Malalas gloss equating Svarog with Hephaestus

attributes.name: golden-haired maidens opening the sky-gates
attributes.notes: The Zoryas are pictured as beautiful virgins, the Morning Zorya opening the sky-gates at dawn and the Evening Zorya closing them at dusk; the Morning Zorya is small and golden-haired.

sources.reference: Russian folklore of the Zorya sisters; Ralston, Songs of the Russian People

attributes.name: the colour red and the thunderstone-axe
attributes.notes: Dongo is associated with the colour red and the stone celt ('thunderstone') hurled to earth in the lightning-strike; his sorko handle the thunder-axe and the ritual fire.

sources.reference: Paul Stoller, Fusion of the Worlds (1989); Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)

attributes.name: river-mother in a copper canoe
attributes.notes: Harakoy Dikko is imagined sailing the Niger in a great copper canoe pushed by Zin-spirits; the river itself is her domain.

sources.reference: Jean Rouch, La religion et la magie songhay (1960)

sacredAnimals.name: cattle of the river
sacredAnimals.notes: Cattle (a 'white cow' in some accounts) are linked to the river-mother as her beasts.

sources.reference: Songhay-Zarma Tooru tradition

attributes.name: armed sun-warrior
attributes.notes: Apolaki, the sun- and war-god, is figured as a warrior; in the myth he and his sister Mayari fight with bamboo clubs until he blinds her in one eye, dividing day from night.

sources.reference: Tagalog/Pampangan myth of Apolaki and Mayari

attributes.name: the maiden who becomes the rice
attributes.notes: Poisoned and buried, Nyi Pohaci's body gives rise to the staple crops: rice from her body, coconut from her head, fruits from her breasts and the sugar-palm from her loins — the dying-maiden origin of cultivated plants.

sources.reference: Wawacan Sulanjana (Sundanese rice-origin manuscript)

sacredPlants.name: rice (pare)
sacredPlants.notes: Rice is her own body and the chief crop sprung from her grave; she is its indwelling soul.

sources.reference: Wawacan Sulanjana

attributes.name: lord of the dark land of Gadlum
attributes.notes: Saragnayan rules the eternally dark realm of Gadlum and keeps charge of the course of the sun; he cannot be slain because his life is hidden outside his body in a wild boar at Paling Bukid.

sources.reference: F. Landa Jocano, Hinilawod

sacredAnimals.name: the wild boar holding his external soul
sacredAnimals.notes: Saragnayan's life-force is lodged in a wild boar; only by killing the boar can he be slain.

sources.reference: F. Landa Jocano, Hinilawod
